questions.question: What is Toolformer's core self-supervised training signal for deciding which tool calls to keep?
options: Human preference ratings on tool call quality
Whether the tool result reduces next-token prediction loss
Whether the tool call succeeds without errors
Whether the tool result is longer than a threshold
questions.explanation: Toolformer (Schick et al., NeurIPS 2023) keeps tool annotations only when executing the tool and including the result reduces loss on the next token. This self-supervised signal requires no human labels.

questions.question: What are the five evaluation categories in BFCL V4, and what is the largest category?
options: Single-turn 40%, Multi-turn 30%, Parallel 10%, Sequential 10%, Hallucination 10%
Agentic 40%, Multi-turn 30%, Live 10%, Non-live 10%, Hallucination 10%
Code 50%, Math 20%, Web 15%, API 10%, Other 5%
Reasoning 40%, Planning 30%, Memory 15%, Tools 10%, Safety 5%
questions.explanation: BFCL V4 (Patil et al., ICML 2025) is composed of: Agentic 40%, Multi-turn 30%, Live 10%, Non-live 10%, Hallucination 10%. Single-turn function calling is now considered near-solved; failures concentrate in the agentic and multi-turn categories.

questions.question: What does 'hallucination detection' mean in the context of BFCL V4?
options: Detecting when the model invents a fact in its response
Detecting when the model should refuse to call any tool because no tool fits the request
Detecting when the model calls a tool with wrong arguments
Detecting when the model calls a tool that has been deprecated
questions.explanation: The hallucination category in BFCL V4 tests whether the model correctly declines to call any tool when the request does not match any available tool. Calling a hallucinated or wrong tool is the failure mode being measured.

questions.question: Why is the tool_use_id field called 'load-bearing' in parallel tool call dispatch?
options: It limits the number of parallel calls to prevent server overload
It ties each tool call to its result, enabling correct routing when multiple calls return out of order
It sets the execution priority of concurrent tool calls
It specifies the timeout for each tool call
questions.explanation: When a model issues multiple parallel tool calls, each has a unique tool_use_id. The runtime uses this ID to route each result back to the correct call. Swapping IDs causes wrong-tool-to-wrong-result routing, a silent but serious failure.

questions.question: What is the most common root cause of wrong-tool-picked failures according to the lesson?
options: Models not having enough parameters
Poor tool descriptions that do not tell the model when to use the tool
Too many tools in the registry
Argument schema being too strict
questions.explanation: Bad tool descriptions are the #1 root cause of wrong-tool-picked failures. The model reads descriptions to choose the right tool; if descriptions do not explain when to use each tool, the model guesses incorrectly.

questions.question: What is the proper handling when a required argument is missing from a model's tool call?
options: Use a default value and proceed silently
Crash the agent with an exception
Return a structured error observation to the model so it can retry with the correct shape
Skip the tool call entirely and continue
questions.explanation: Missing required fields should return a structured error observation back to the model describing what is missing. This enables the model to retry with the correct schema rather than causing a crash.
